name: Obsidian-Pulpit
geological_features: Elevated lava plateaus connected by magma channels
specific_features: A massive volcanic neck formation rising 8 km above the surrounding plain
Lava tube system connecting multiple active volcanic centers
description: Obsidian-Pulpit is dominated by a single geological feature of commanding presence: a volcanic neck formation rising eight kilometers above the surrounding basalt plains, the exposed magma conduit of an ancient volcano whose cone has long since eroded away. The neck is composed of dense, columnar basalt that resists the erosion claiming the softer surrounding rock, standing as a solitary monument to volcanic forces that shaped this world's surface. The plains around it are sheets of obsidian glass, cooled lava flows frozen into mirrors that reflect the glow of active fissure eruptions on the horizon.

The toxic atmosphere is a sulfurous mix that corrodes exposed metal and reduces visibility during eruption events to arm's length. Heat is omnipresent, the ground itself warm to the touch even in the coolest regions, the obsidian plains radiating stored thermal energy long after the flows that created them have solidified. The volcanic neck catches updrafts of hot, toxic gas that spiral around its flanks, creating a permanent haze that gives the formation a ghostly, ethereal appearance against the orange-lit sky.

The lava tube network that connects the planet's active volcanic centers is extensive enough to serve as a sheltered transit system, the tubes maintaining relatively stable temperatures and protecting travelers from the worst of the surface conditions. Survey teams have mapped over three thousand kilometers of navigable tubes, some large enough to accommodate mining vehicles, their walls lined with mineral deposits concentrated by the passage of countless lava flows. The tubes are not without hazard, however, as partial collapses and sudden magma influxes have claimed equipment and nearly claimed lives.

Chromium and vanadium deposits on Obsidian-Pulpit are of exceptional purity, concentrated by the same volcanic processes that built the landscape. The volcanic neck itself contains the richest veins, the dense basalt having acted as a trap for metallic minerals precipitating from the magma. Mining the neck is a technical challenge the low gravity helps with, but the heat and toxic atmosphere make sustained surface operations costly. Automated extraction systems work the most accessible deposits while engineering teams evaluate the feasibility of deep-core mining into the neck's interior, where the highest-grade ores are believed to lie.
